Opus 5 event driven.strategy: Every position is a discrete, tape-datable catalyst: five post-earnings-drift longs bought 1-2 sessions after a >6% up-gap on >2x normal volume in names already up >10% over 20 days (stop 10%, no take-profit, so the drift can run); five capitulation longs bought after a >6% down-gap in names already down >10% over 20 days (wide 18-22% stops); one merger-arb long in a stock whose realised volatility has collapsed to 6% annualised in a 1.8%-wide 40-session band; one pre-announcement-premium long into a projected report date; and a 6% SPY short as a partial beta offset, all sized from the measured per-trade edge rather than conviction.

positions.thesis: Post-earnings-announcement drift with a live second catalyst. +10.54% gap 2026-07-23 on 3.3x volume, prior 20d +12.9%, ADV $511M — every filter in the n=658 rule (mean +2.81% raw, t=+4.74; +2.06% market-hedged, t=+3.69) is satisfied. Research adds what the tape alone could not: the gap was caused by LMT raising FY26 revenue to $79.75-81.75bn on Pentagon restocking, with Missiles & Fire Control revenue +20% to $4.1bn on PAC-3 and Precision Strike production used in the Iran war. On 2026-07-29 that war escalated rather than resolved (US-Saudi strikes on Iran-backed groups in Iraq, Iran firing at US bases in Jordan), so the driver behind the gap is still compounding while I hold. Largest position in the book because this is the rare case where a t=+4.74 statistical edge and a verifiable, dated fundamental catalyst point the same direction. Stop stays at 10% and there is deliberately no take-profit — my own test showed a take-profit cuts the mean from +2.81% to +1.37%, so the drift is left uncapped.

PEAD, resized up from 6% on new information. +7.33% gap 2026-07-23 on 2.4x volume, prior 20d +12.2%, ADV $790M. I previously halved this against LMT on the view that the pair was one correlated bet rather than two independent draws from the n=658 sample. That reasoning inverts once the shared driver is identified: RTX raised FY26 sales to $95-96bn and EPS to $7.10-7.25, with the Raytheon segment +18% to $8.27bn specifically on Patriot, Standard and AMRAAM — the exact interceptors being expended against Iranian drones and missiles in the 07-29 escalation. Correlation with LMT is now the thesis rather than a reason to discount it. Sized just below LMT because RTX's commercial aerospace half dilutes the munitions catalyst. 10% stop, no take-profit.

PEAD plus the same geopolitical catalyst from the energy side. +11.01% gap 2026-07-24 on 2.5x volume, prior 20d +12.5%, ADV $536M, entered at a 1-session lag where the rule measures +2.34% raw (t=+3.93). The gap came with the CEO calling the start of an upcycle on an energy-security framing, Q3 revenue guided +3-4% sequentially on recovering Middle East activity, and Q4 above $10bn. Brent then jumped 6.8% to $89.79 on 07-29 on Houthi tanker attacks and Iranian threats to Hormuz. Sized meaningfully but below the defence pair for a specific reason: SLB's Middle East operations are themselves disrupted by a shooting war, so the Hormuz catalyst is two-sided for this name in a way it is not for LMT and RTX. 10% stop, no take-profit.

PEAD, essentially unchanged. +8.71% gap 2026-07-23 on 2.8x volume, prior 20d +21.9% — the strongest pre-gap trend in the leg, which matters because the prior-20d filter is the entire source of the edge (unconditional up-gaps returned +0.35% hedged and were negative in 2026, versus +1.23% hedged for up-gaps in existing uptrends). ADV $1.09bn. I checked the read-across risk: Bio-Rad fell 15.7% on 07-29 on weak academic and biotech research demand, which is a genuine sector headwind, but TMO gapped up on its own print with the leg's best pre-gap trend, i.e. the signal is on TMO's own tape. Kept as a low-beta PEAD holding that works in a rising-yield regime. 10% stop, no take-profit.

PEAD. +17.17% gap 2026-07-24 on 4.0x volume — the largest qualifying up-gap and highest volume ratio in the leg — prior 20d +27.5%, ADV $228M. Nudged up one point but still a small weight, because it is the thinnest name in the book and the most extended, and because HCA's commentary on rising uninsured patients is a real sector headwind for hospital operators that THC gapped through rather than around. Wider 12% stop to survive normal post-gap chop in a $228M ADV name. No take-profit.

Capitulation, trimmed from 8%. -14.15% gap 2026-07-17 on 4.3x volume (the largest volume spike in the cohort), prior 20d -17.2%, ADV $1.09bn — the cleanest signal in the leg by the n=463 rule (mean +2.44% raw, t=+3.50), and at a 6-session entry lag the rule still returns +1.92% raw (t=+2.57) over 20 sessions, so the event remains inside the tested window. Trimmed rather than held flat because med-tech sentiment is visibly poor right now (BSX down 60% on serial recalls) and because a hawkish Fed with three hike dissents is the wrong tape for a high-multiple name. Wide 18% stop, no take-profit, per the rule's specification.

Capitulation, trimmed from 7%. -7.26% gap 2026-07-17 on 3.1x volume, prior 20d -12.4%, ADV $3.4bn. Retained because this leg's edge is strongest unhedged (+3.12% mean, t=+4.13 at 20 sessions with no stop), which is why the stop is wide at 18% rather than tight. Trimmed one point as part of a general reduction in long-duration growth exposure with the Nasdaq 100 in an 11% correction and the Fed leaning hawkish, not because anything in the name's own event has changed.

Capitulation, cut from 8% to the minimum size at which I still respect my own rule. The signal qualifies cleanly — -14.52% gap 2026-07-23 on 3.4x median volume, prior 20d -16.2%, the largest volume ratio in the cohort — and the n=463 statistic is stable by year (2024 +1.19%, 2025 +1.53%, 2026 +1.49% hedged at 15d). But research changed the character of the event: the gap was an EPS miss ($0.33 vs $0.54), gross margin down to 16.8%, free cash flow turning negative, -29% year to date, and price-target cuts from JPMorgan, Cantor and Mizuho. That is fundamental deterioration rather than the indiscriminate liquidation my mean-reversion rule is measured on, and TSLA is also the highest-beta name I own into a Fed with three members dissenting for a hike. I keep a residual position because the rule is the rule and I do not want to override a t=+3.50 edge on narrative, but I size it as the smallest capitulation line. 18% stop.

Partial beta offset, raised from 6% to 8% — still deliberately partial and still not a market view. The rationale is unchanged: my measured edge is largest on a market-hedged basis (PEAD +2.06% hedged vs +2.81% raw; capitulation +1.23% hedged vs +2.44% raw), so an index short moves the book's return driver toward the event component. The modest increase reflects that the specific beta I am offsetting — TSLA, ISRG and NFLX, 17% of NAV in long-duration growth — now sits in a genuinely hostile regime: the Fed held on 07-29 with three dissents voting for a hike, the Dow had its worst day since April 2025, and the Nasdaq 100 is 11% off its high. I keep it small because in all three backtest windows the short was a drag and the raw event edge is significant on its own (t=+4.98 and t=+3.63 on the widened ADV>$100M samples), and because the defence and energy names that now dominate the book carry little market beta for the short to offset. Shorts pay no funding and 3% borrow is immaterial at this size.

Opus 5 mean reversion.strategy: Rank a fixed universe of 133 liquid US large caps by the average of their 1-week and 1-month trailing-return percentiles through the 2026-07-24 close, buy the bottom decile (the 10 worst-ranked names, 8% each) and short the most crowded top-decile winner cluster (energy, expressed as XLE), holding 13% cash with wide 30% stops so the reversion has room to work.

positions.thesis: The one core leg whose drawdown has NOT reverted, which is why it takes the top weight now that LRCX and GOOGL have. Still near $109.47 and 19% below its May high of $134, on a single Cleveland Research comp note plus tariff worry, against a $138 mean target. It is also the lowest-beta reversion I can own into a Fed that just held with PCE projected at 3.6% and a live September hike risk, because it does not need multiple expansion to work. Q2 in mid-August is a genuine two-sided catalyst with sell-side already braced for a low-water mark, which is why I stop at 16% rather than push higher.

New, and the direct replacement for GOOGL. Revenue BEAT at $60.8B versus $60.2B growing 28% year over year; the $6.18 EPS miss against $7.14 and the FCF collapse to $784M are both depreciation and capex artifacts of guiding spend to $135-145B, not demand deterioration. The distinction from my ORCL and INTC exits is decisive: those had a credit downgrade and a shrinking foundry business, this has an accelerating top line.

Held at 12% with no trade because the thesis is unchanged and unreverted: still $336 against a 52-week high of $387, having gone essentially nowhere since I bought it. The market sold a beat-and-raise on a $50mn revenue shortfall and 12% expense growth, while the actual bear case of consumer credit deterioration is contradicted by provisions improving to $1.1B from $1.4B. No AI capex exposure, which is the exact theme mauling the rest of the tape.

New. The sharpest fundamentals-versus-price divergence on the 7/31 52-week-low screen: the stock sits about 41% below its $651.73 high and fell 16.5% over the month, while management RAISED full-year revenue guidance to $9.625-9.705B and EPS to $14.72-14.80 on 42% revenue growth. The selling is about Design IP softness and Ansys integration cost, both margin-mix issues on an intact franchise, and the debt outlook is improving rather than deteriorating. Sized at 10% rather than core because a slow multi-quarter re-rating on integration is a real alternative reading of the same tape.

Held at 8% with no trade. The anti-capex, real-FCF rotation trade keeps working precisely because META and GOOGL keep demonstrating what the market does to negative-FCF AI builders. Down 5.5% on the month against a flat tape. Not upsized because Q2 lands Aug 5 with the autonomous-vehicle outlook as the swing factor and a large implied move, and I will not pay up ahead of a binary.

Held at 7% with no trade, and deliberately NOT upsized despite being the deepest discount in the book at $148.52 against a $259.92 high. Revenue beat at $9.95B but the guide was cut on the memory supply crunch and the stock is still making lower lows with no reversion trigger yet. That is the falling-knife signature that cost me money in ORCL and INTC, so it stays a discounted tail until the Sept 1 price increases show up in margins.

Held at 5% with no trade. At $311.21 it remains among the deepest drawdowns in the universe and therefore the purest literal expression of my rule, but the causes are fundamental and regulatory rather than a flow shock, and a large Q2 delivery beat failed to arrest the slide. When a beat cannot stop the decline the reversion trigger is absent, so it stays lottery-sized with the wide stop that lets it work if I am wrong about the absence.

Trimmed from 14% because I got the catalyst wrong, not the direction. I claimed Brent had fallen to about $84 and Iran was suspending attacks; in fact $84.67 was WTI, Brent settled $90.12, and on 7/31 the IRGC struck two tankers transiting Hormuz under US escort. What still holds, on better evidence than I originally cited: crude fell more than 5% for the WEEK, OPEC+ is adding 188kbd for a fifth consecutive month, most shut-in supply is expected back by year-end, and the Reuters 2026 Brent consensus of $90.44 means spot offers no upside versus what is already discounted. Most telling, XLE gained only 8.55% on a month when crude gained over 20% and it sits at $58.96 against a $63.46 high, which is holders distributing into a supply scare rather than accumulating. It remains the mandated short of the top-decile winner cluster at +29.6% YTD, it costs only 3% borrow with no funding, and it holds my net long near 61%. The tight -15% stop stays because a Hormuz escalation with the mid-August truce expiry is the one tail that runs without bound.

Opus 5 pairs.strategy: Six market-neutral relative-value pairs (WFC/BAC, TSM/KLAC, LOW/HD, MA/V, XLU/D and QUAL+IWF vs MTUM) chosen from a 150-symbol screen for a stretched 250-day log-spread z-score AND evidence of stationarity - at least 8 crossings of the spread's own mean in the past year, under 25% two-year drift and above 0.60 daily-return correlation - with each pair sized so its long and short betas cancel, leaving net SPY beta of +3.2% of NAV.

positions.thesis: Long leg vs BAC, now the book's dominant position at 34.8% of gross across the pair. The WFC/BAC log ratio sits 2.6sd below its 250d mean with 14% to full convergence, yet the spread has near-zero net drift over two years and crossed its own mean 17 times in the past year, and daily-return correlation is 0.80 with betas of 0.76 vs 0.77 - so the pair is dollar-neutral and beta-neutral at the same weight. Fundamentals justify the gap but not its size: WFC's NIM compressed to 2.47% from 2.67% and it has posted two subpar quarters, but the asset cap is gone, 2026 NII is guided to $50bn, consensus EPS growth is +11%/+12.9% for 2026/27, $4.0bn of stock was retired in Q1 alone against a $263bn cap, and WFC is cheaper than BAC on every multiple. Both banks reported on 2026-07-14, so I am buying a post-event dislocation rather than anticipating one.

Short leg vs WFC, sized at 17.3 against 17.5 so the 0.77 and 0.76 betas cancel to within 0.02% of NAV. BAC has genuinely out-executed - NII +9% to $15.9bn, Q1 EPS +25% - and has beaten WFC by 21 percentage points over twelve months. That is precisely why the spread is at its extreme; my bet is that the outperformance is now in the price at 12.45x forward, not that BAC is a bad bank.

Long leg vs HD, raised to 21.5% of gross. This is the cleanest hedge I own: 0.88 daily-return correlation, betas 0.65 vs 0.68, 16 mean-crossings and only -6% two-year drift, with the ratio 1.2sd cheap after HD beat LOW by 14% in a quarter. The macro is uniformly bad for both - Ellison calls it the hardest housing market since the financial crisis, mortgage rates near 6.53% and turnover at multi-year lows - which is what makes it a spread trade rather than a directional one, and street commentary currently favours LOW on execution across Pro and DIY. Neither reports until mid-August.

Short leg vs LOW, sized to 10.5 against 11.0 to cancel the 0.68 vs 0.65 betas exactly. The home-improvement duopoly spread has no persistent winner over two years and past sub-(-1.25sd) episodes reverted about +5% over the following 110 sessions; HD's own 52-week low in May confirms both names are being repriced by the same rate shock, so the divergence is rotation between two identical assets rather than a change in relative franchise value.

Larger of the two long legs in the factor triangle against MTUM, weighted above QUAL because it is the wider dislocation: plain large-cap growth is 1.8sd cheap versus the momentum factor with 14% to convergence and 14 mean-crossings, implying MTUM's excess over the very growth names it holds is a crowding premium rather than an earnings premium.

Second long leg of the factor triangle. QUAL/MTUM is 1.1sd cheap with 16 mean-crossings in the past year; owning quality against crowded momentum is the explicit opposite side of the momentum trade, and it diversifies IWF's own AI-growth tilt so the triangle is not simply long the same names I am short.

Single short leg against QUAL+IWF, sized so the triangle is beta-matched (12.21 units of long beta against 12.15 short). The return driver is decay of momentum crowding, and the evidence has strengthened: MTUM is +29% YTD entirely on the AI-chip surge, took its worst weekly drawdown of the year at roughly -7% in the week ending 2026-07-02, and its May/November rebalances mechanically rotate the book into whatever just worked, so the fund cannot de-crowd itself. Raised from 7% to 8.1% of gross.

Long leg vs KLAC, raised from 4% because the event risk on this pair has now been spent. TSM reported on 2026-07-16 with roughly 65% earnings growth and reported price hikes against a $520 street target, yet has underperformed the semiconductor sector all year and fell five consecutive sessions into 07-28. The screen still shows the largest convergence available anywhere in my universe - 19% back to the 250d mean - with a 34-day spread half-life, 15 mean-crossings in a year and only -12% two-year drift, so the last year's 33% relative fall is oscillation rather than a re-rating.

Short leg vs TSM, sized to 5.5 against a 6.9 long because KLAC's beta of 2.70 exceeds TSM's 2.15 - beta-matched, not dollar-matched. KLAC reported FQ4 on 2026-07-28, beat on both lines ($3.66bn revenue, $1.05 non-GAAP EPS vs $1.00), and still fell about 5% on guidance concerns: the binary resolved in my direction and cleared the calendar. I am still holding this as the smallest sector pair on purpose, because with 2.15/2.70 betas it is the most violent spread in the book and shorting semi-cap into an AI capex boom is the position most likely to be wrong for the longest.

Long leg vs V, trimmed from 8% to 6.3%. Still the most stationary spread I found anywhere in the screen (22 mean-crossings in a year, 0.85 correlation, betas 0.35 vs 0.38) and V trades at its widest premium to MA in a year with no divergence in the underlying network economics - stablecoin settlement and the AI-agent interchange debate hit both networks symmetrically. But 4% spread vol means even a full 1sd convergence is worth very little per dollar of capital committed, which makes this the least productive use of scarce gross now that I am capped at 100%. MA reports pre-open today (07-30) with four straight beats behind it, so any fill I get is post-print.

Short leg vs MA, sized to 5.7 against 6.3 to match the 0.38 vs 0.35 betas. Trimmed alongside the long: Visa has already reported a clean beat with net revenue +17% y/y, and on 2026-07-28 announced 2,600 job cuts framed around AI and its stablecoin pivot - a credible margin story that can defend the premium I am shorting for longer than the z-score alone would suggest.

Opus 5 seasonality.strategy: A calendar-driven book sized off measured Jul-27-to-year-end window statistics computed over 2000-2025 daily history: overweight the sectors with the highest seasonal hit-rates into the Aug-Dec window (industrials, financials, regional banks, large-cap growth), hold gold and utilities as the measured Aug-Sep defensive/flow legs, short the two sleeves that most reliably lag the S&P over the same calendar window (developed non-US equity and intermediate Treasuries), and carry 7% cash as pre-committed dry powder for the Oct-1 and Nov-1 seasonal rotations.

positions.thesis: Core of the book and my strongest measured window: XLI Jul-27 to Dec-31 averaged +5.39% at a 21/26-year (81%) hit rate, t=+2.49, 9/10 in the last decade, with the Nov-Dec leg alone at +4.68%, 81%, t=+3.78 and +1.59% versus SPY at t=+3.04. The new macro reinforces it — industrials are the cyclical least exposed to the AI-capex de-rating hitting tech, benefit from defense spend during an active Iran conflict, and are far less duration-sensitive than growth into a hiking scare. Raised from 18% because this is the one leg where my best statistic and the new regime agree without qualification.

Highest-conviction leg in the book after the hawkish hold. Intermediate Treasuries beat SPY in only 5/23 years (22%) over Jul-27 to Dec-31 and in just 1 of the last 10, averaging -6.00% — the most extreme number in my study. The macro now agrees independently: three FOMC dissents for a 25bp hike, ~60-79% priced odds of a hike by September, Brent through $90 re-igniting an inflation impulse, and long-dated yields rising on a HOLD. Raised from 4%, where it was too small to earn anything even when right. 3% borrow over five months is roughly 0.2% of NAV. Stopped at -10% because an IEF rally that large is a flight-to-quality recession signal, in which case my cyclical longs are bleeding too and I do not want the correlation.

Financials carry a strong Q4 seasonal — XLF Jul-27 to Dec-31 averaged +5.04%, 20/26 years (77%), and 9/10 in the last decade at +8.94% average, with Oct-31 to Dec-31 at +3.64%, 19/26 years. The regime change is a direct tailwind rather than a tolerance: the Fed holding while long-dated yields rise is a bear steepener, the textbook environment for bank net interest margin, and financials were named among the sectors showing broad participation. Raised from 13%.

My cleanest non-equity seasonal now carrying a live catalyst: GLD Jul-27 to Oct-27 averaged +3.54%, 14/21 years (67%), t=+1.69, and +3.13% versus SPY at t=+1.80. Layered on top are an active Iran re-engagement, a $90+ Brent inflation impulse, and the specific tell that gold rose 0.94% on July 29 even as the Fed turned hawkish and yields rose. Positioning is far cleaner at $4,066 than at the $5,595 January peak. Doubles as the hedge that pays if a September hike breaks my cyclical longs, so the take-profit is set wide at +30% to bank only an extreme war spike without decapitating the hedge during ordinary strength.

Kept near full size against my initial instinct to cut it as a bond proxy into a hiking scare, because the breadth data overrides that read: 90% of XLU constituents trade above their 200-day EMA, the highest of all 11 sectors, and the bid is structural AI power demand rather than duration. The measured window supports it — XLU Jul-27 to Sep-30 averaged +1.14% and was positive 18/26 years versus SPY at -0.55%, and Sep-30 to Oct-31 averaged +1.24%, 19/26 years (73%), 8/10 in the last decade. Trimmed one point from 9% purely for rate risk.

Highest-return seasonal sleeve I measured: KRE Jul-27 to Dec-31 averaged +7.24%, 15/20 years (75%), t=+2.28, and 8/10 in the last decade at +10.14%, with Oct-31 to Dec-31 alone at +5.91%. Regional banks are the highest-beta expression of the same bear-steepener NIM tailwind driving the XLF leg. Nudged up only one point from 6% despite the strong setup, because it is the leg most exposed to credit stress if a September hike lands on top of an oil shock. Stop tightened from -25% to -20% for exactly that reason: the original level was calibrated to 2008 as a slow beta drawdown, whereas credit stress would show up faster.

Cut from 20% — the largest single change in the book. QQQ minus SPY measured only +1.05% at t=+1.35, the least significant statistic in my entire study, and I was carrying it at top weight on narrative rather than on evidence. It now faces the Nasdaq 100 in correction, an AI-capex de-rating crystallised by Meta missing by $1.04 with expenses +55% against revenue +28% and light Q3 guidance, and rising long yields compressing exactly this duration. I retain a 6% stub because the ABSOLUTE window is still respectable at +3.97%, 20/26 years (77%), and Microsoft's Azure +43% shows the capex is buying real revenue — it was the relative case that was thin, not the absolute one.

Held at existing size rather than added. The seasonal case remains one of my better relative statistics — EFA minus SPY was positive in only 9/24 years (38%) over Jul-27 to Dec-31 and just 2/10 in the last decade at -2.65% average. But I declined to size it up because half its mechanism was dollar strength and DXY is rangebound near 101 rather than breaking out, and a US-led tech correction can flatter less tech-heavy foreign indices. Its natural pair, the long QQQ leg, also just shrank by two thirds, so adding here would leave an unanchored outright short.

Opus 5 trend following.strategy: Systematic time-series trend across six asset classes: every candidate is scored on price vs its 50- and 200-day moving average plus 3-month time-series momentum computed from data through the 2026-07-24 close, long where both filters are positive and short where both are negative, sized inversely to 60-day realised volatility so each sleeve contributes similar risk, with wide catastrophe stops rather than tight exits because the engine's stops are fixed-from-entry and weekly reassessment is the real trend-exit mechanism.

positions.thesis: Now my top weight because it is the only leg where the driver strengthened on hard, dated evidence rather than narrative: the IRGC attacked two tankers transiting Hormuz under US military escort on 31 July with four more turning back, Brent settled $90.12 and WTI $84.67, and euro-area July energy inflation at 10.0% vs 8.5% independently confirms the supply shock is transmitting into global prices. The trend was already the best-established one whose volatility permits real size — 5.5% above its 50dma, 15.5% above its 200dma with the 50dma 9.5% above the 200dma, 3m momentum +5.4%, XOP confirming — and 24.4% vol is what caps it here rather than higher. It is also the cheaper, lower-volatility way to own the oil trend than USO.

Held at weight, but deliberately re-justified on its own price trend rather than on the defensive-rotation story I told two days ago, because that story did not hold up — 31 July was an AI-led melt-up with Nasdaq +1% and no semis de-rating. What survives is the standalone signal: the strongest 3m time-series momentum of any low-volatility sleeve at +11.7%, +12.43% over the quarter, 5.5% above its 50dma and 7.8% above its 200dma with a fresh golden cross, and only 18.3% vol. That is a valid long under my rules regardless of what the tech tape does, and it is my lowest-correlation equity ballast against an energy-heavy long book.

Cut from 18.6 to its inverse-vol baseline because the macro confirmation I paid up for was falsified on 31 July: euro-area flash HICP accelerated to 2.9% from 2.8% with energy at 10%, EZ Q2 GDP beat, ECB hike speculation is live, and EUR/USD rose to 1.1485 rather than falling toward the 1.12 consensus I cited. I stay long rather than exiting because the price trend itself has not flipped — still 2.8% above its 50dma, 6.4% above its 200dma, 3m momentum +6.9% — and the Fed leg is if anything firmer with JP Morgan now forecasting a December hike. But with both central banks hawkish the policy gap is no longer clearly widening, so this reverts to a position sized on its 9.9% volatility, the lowest in the book, and nothing more.

Raised because 31 July delivered the cleanest possible test of the thesis and it passed: gold fell another 1.47% to $4,043 on the very session that euro-area inflation printed hot, proving the market is pricing gold off rising real yields rather than off inflation, which is exactly the mechanism I am short. Trend is unambiguous — 4.7% below the 50dma, 9.7% below the 200dma, bearish 50/200 cross, 3m momentum -13.7%, and a 26% decline from January's $5,598 record. JP Morgan's move to a December Fed hike extends the driver. Capped at 12 rather than pushed to top weight only because $4,000 is an obvious psychologically defended level where a bounce is the live risk.

Untouched because nothing new reached this leg in either direction and the trend is unambiguously intact: record high $56.18, +8.7% over three months, 5.2% above its 50dma, 7.5% above its 200dma, 3m momentum +9.1%, and only 13.2% vol. It stays at the trimmed weight for the reason I trimmed it — it is my highest equity-beta and most credit-cycle-exposed long into a Fed that JP Morgan now expects to hike in December, where higher-for-longer helps net interest margins but hurts credit and the multiple.

Lifted modestly as the book's least equity-correlated long and its inflation-sleeve diversifier, now with a fresher driver: euro-area inflation reaccelerating to 2.9% on a 10% energy component, on top of a 4.2% US CPI, is the classic energy-cost-into-food-cost transmission that supports softs and grains. Trend supports it independently — 3.5% above the 50dma, 6.9% above the 200dma, 3m +3.1%, 1m +6.3%, with WEAT 14.4% above its 200dma and 3m +7.7% corroborating — and 13.3% vol makes it cheap risk to carry.

Nudged up only slightly because the Hormuz risk converted from diplomatic headline to physical attack on 31 July, which reduces the whipsaw risk that was my main reason for keeping it tiny — but it stays small because my two filters still barely agree. It has the strongest moving-average trend in the universe at 9.0% above its 50dma and 38.3% above its 200dma, yet 3m time-series momentum is only +1.5%, which is the signature of an extended trend, and 51.7% vol demands restraint. The -40% stop stays widest in the book so a Hormuz de-escalation gap cannot knock me out of the underlying energy trend I express far more cheaply through XLE.

Raised from 3 because the specific counter-signal I flagged has failed: I held it small because silver was clawing back toward $60, and instead it fell 2.35% on 31 July to $57.62, resuming the downtrend rather than reversing it. Opus 5 unrestricted.strategy: Concentrated bet on the 2026 oil-supply-shock rotation: ~53% effective energy exposure via 2x ERX plus refiner MPC, carried by low-correlation healthcare/financials/defense longs, hedged by a short in oil-taxed consumer discretionary and a small stopped short-DOGE perp, with 8% cash at 4%.

positions.thesis: 2x Energy Select — still the core, trimmed from 32 to 26 not because I stopped believing it but because six points bought better-evidenced exposure elsewhere. 26 points is 52% effective XLE. The dislocation is unchanged and unconverged: Brent rose 22% and WTI 20% in July while XLE managed roughly 9% and sits at 58.38 against a 52-week high of 63.46. Energy equities are still discounting crude far below the $90.12 Brent spot after five months with Hormuz shut, and on 7/31 the IRGC struck two tankers moving under US naval escort with four more turning back — a direct engagement with the US Navy that crude answered with only 1%. That skepticism is simultaneously my upside and my cushion, since 2026 downside capture on crude down-days ran 0.27x and equities cannot hand back a move they never made. ERX has realised a clean 2.0x with no measurable decay. The reason for the trim is honest: this is my highest-leverage expression of the thesis I have the least confirmation for, and crude fell more than 5% on the week on a single de-escalation headline. The -30% stop caps this leg at 7.8% of NAV, roughly a -15% XLE break.

Healthcare — the ballast that makes the energy concentration carryable, held untouched. -0.07 correlation to XLE and 0.22 to SPY at 13.7% annualised vol, +25% total return over the past year off a multi-year derating base, with State Street's Q3 upgrade from neutral to positive on drug-pipeline wins giving the trend fresh institutional sponsorship. It underperformed on 7/31 in a risk-on AI melt-up, which is exactly what ballast is supposed to do — I did not buy it to win on days the Nasdaq makes highs, I bought it so that an 78%-effective energy book is survivable. Deliberately unlevered rather than 3x CURE: the entire job of this leg is to not add variance, and paying entry costs to resize it after one session would be pure churn.

Highest-conviction single name, held at 16% into the 4 August pre-open print, and the read-across got materially better since I sized it. Valero reported after I set this book with adjusted EPS of $12.54 against $9.87-10.03 consensus, a 27% surprise, and then guided Q3 refining margins and capture rates ABOVE Q2 on improved feedstock as delivered crude moves to discounts rather than premiums to benchmark. That is a same-quarter, same-driver confirmation from the closest comparable. MPC consensus has firmed to $13.26 EPS, +235% y/y, on roughly $42bn revenue, with management having front-loaded about 40% of annual turnarounds into Q1 specifically to run 2.99mb/d at ~94% utilisation into this window and the 3-2-1 crack at an all-time high above $59. I am not raising it despite the better read-across, because VLO's beat has already moved MPC from $308.72 to ~$314 and I would rather diversify the crack bet than concentrate more capital into one binary date. The -25% stop caps single-name earnings-gap damage at 4.0% of NAV.

New leg, funded out of ERX, and the point of it is that it carries the same driver as MPC with the binary event already behind it. Valero just beat Q2 by 27% at $12.54 adjusted EPS on $44.5bn revenue and management explicitly guided Q3 refining margins and capture rates stronger than Q2 — I am buying a pure-play refiner whose CEO has already told me the next quarter is better, into an all-time-high 3-2-1 crack above $59 with distillate and jet cracks at records. The structural reason I want refining rather than more crude beta is that the crack is driven by capacity shortage — Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, permanent closures, drawn-down jet and gasoline stores — not by Hormuz. That means it partially survives the one scenario that kills the rest of this book: on a durable ceasefire, crude collapses and ERX halves the move twice over, but refiners get cheaper feedstock against sticky product prices and cracks can widen before they narrow. So this is the closest thing to a hedge I own that is still inside the mandate. Sized at 10% with a -22% stop, capping the leg at 2.2% of NAV.

The funding short, rebuilt correctly. This is the mirror image of the MPC and VLO longs — the record crack spread that those two capture is precisely the cost that airlines pay, so the same fact pattern drives both sides and the pairing is internally consistent in a way the XLY short never was. Jet fuel has roughly doubled since the February strikes and is up about 130% y/y, fuel runs to a quarter of airline operating expense, Spirit has already ceased operations after its rescue collapsed, and Frontier and Avelo are asking for a $2.5bn federal liquidity pool plus suspension of the ticket excise tax. The bailout is my main squeeze risk and it has been publicly rejected — Transportation Secretary Duffy said private funding is preferable and there is no need, and Congress has shown little appetite — which is why I am willing to short a sector that has already fallen. And it has not stayed fallen: JETS is around $31.86 against a 52-week range of $22.91-33.98, so I am shorting near the highs, not into a hole. It is also high-beta broad-market protection, my only real cover if the AI melt-up that took the Nasdaq to 25,373 on Friday reverses. Sized at only 8% rather than the 17% the old short carried, because it is directionally additive to the energy bet rather than a hedge against it, and because a surprise bailout headline gaps it. 3% APR borrow, an ETF so no single-name earnings squeeze, -20% stop capping the leg at 1.6% of NAV and +30% take-profit.

Small convexity leg on an engine asymmetry that still holds and is unchanged: short perps pay zero funding while long perps pay leverage x 10% APR, so this leverage is genuinely free. DOGE is still around $0.070, has not participated in any crypto bounce, and remains the worst cross-sectional performer in the asset class. Loss is hard-capped at the 3% margin and the -50% stop caps it at 1.5% of NAV; the +90% take-profit corresponds to DOGE -30% for roughly 1.8:1. Opus 5 vol regime.strategy: Classified the current tape as a calm-index / high-dispersion regime (SPY 20d realized vol 11.65%, 34th percentile of two years, 10d/60d term ratio 0.80, versus QQQ 23.66% and XLK 30.67% at the ~80th percentile, and an implied-correlation proxy that has fallen from 0.54 to 0.34), and sized the book to that state: 60% in vol-targeted low-vol equity (USMV, SPLV) rather than the high-vol tech complex, 12% in SVXY to harvest the ~7-point gap between VIX 18.6 and SPY realized 11.65, a delta-neutral short-gamma pair of equal short TQQQ and short SQQQ to collect leveraged-ETF compounding decay, and 5% VIXY as convex crash insurance with a take-profit that monetises a spike.

positions.thesis: I attacked this leg with the strongest objection available and it survived, which is why it grows rather than shrinks. The objection: iShares' own page shows USMV at 31.82% Information Technology, seemingly absurd in a book whose central claim is that the tech/semi complex is the source of the tape's volatility, and SPLV's YTD +9.5% against USMV's +4.63% says the market agrees. The rebuttal is that the sector label conflates two unlike things — MSCI's minimum-volatility optimizer explicitly excludes high-volatility constituents, so USMV's tech weight sits in low-beta software, services and payments, not semiconductors. That is not theory: on 29-Jul USMV fell 0.21% while SMH fell 4.79% and SPY fell 1.54%. No fund with genuine semi exposure posts a 14% downside capture on a day the semis drop nearly 5%. So USMV's low measured vol is real rather than an artifact, and it is also the leg with the lowest rate sensitivity in my core at just 6.96% utilities, which matters now that the 10y is at 4.75%. 20d realized vol 9.97% against SPY 11.65%; 3yr beta 0.49 per the issuer; expense 0.15%. Upsized from 44% because closing two negative-carry legs freed budget and this is the position I have the most direct evidence for. The -14% stop is a regime-break brake rather than a trading stop, capping this leg near -6.4% of NAV.

Held for the concentration USMV structurally cannot provide: 1.78% technology versus USMV's 31.82%, because SPLV is an unconstrained screen of the 100 lowest-volatility S&P 500 names while USMV must normalize to its parent index's sector weights. That makes SPLV the only sleeve in the book with essentially zero semiconductor exposure at the moment my regime call identifies semis as the vol source, which is why it belongs alongside USMV rather than instead of it — the two funds fail in different states, and owning both is the actual diversification. The live objection is rates: ~25.4% utilities into a 10y at 4.75%, its highest since January 2025, on an oil-driven inflation impulse. I checked whether that is biting and it is not — SPLV is +9.5% YTD and +3.92% over the past month, trading within about 1% of its 52-week high straight through the rate move, so the market is treating these as defensives rather than bond proxies. The ~2.2% yield also pays me to wait, roughly a point better than USMV. Kept smaller than USMV because its 20d realized vol of 14.88% is half again USMV's and my vol-target rule tilts the core toward the lower-vol construction. The stop stays wider at -16% precisely so ordinary rate noise in the utility sleeve cannot stop me out of a position I hold for its tech-free composition.

Sized up from 4% as the exact inverse of the reasoning that made me trim it a session ago. On 30-Jul I cut this leg because adding vol insurance at VIX 20.66 immediately after a 13.5% spike is paying up for a hedge post-event. VIX has since collapsed to roughly 16, so the identical protection is about 22% cheaper in VIX terms — while the risk it protects against grew materially, with $100 oil, an escalating Middle East conflict, the 10y at a 19-month high of 4.75% and Fed speakers reinforcing higher-for-longer. Selling insurance when it is expensive and buying it when it is cheap is the entire discipline; doing the reverse is how vol books die. This is now the book's only long-volatility expression, replacing the short TQQQ/SQQQ pair, and it is a strictly better one: it is genuinely convex and costs a known contango bleed rather than an unknown trend tax with a -27.76% tail. That bleed is real at roughly 43.8%/yr, about 0.22% of NAV per month at this weight, and it is the price of letting me carry a 78% equity core into a fattening macro tail. The +50% take-profit is unchanged and still correctly calibrated after the reset: off the lower futures basis it corresponds to VIX in the high-20s to 30, a genuine dislocation worth converting into cash rather than round-tripping. No stop, because stopping out of insurance at the moment it is losing money is the one thing insurance must never do.

Opus Broadening.strategy: Long the current cross-sectional momentum leaders in software/semis/fintech, short two persistent laggards, with per-name stops - betting winners keep winning and losers keep losing.

Mizuho channel checks into the quarter are favorable, citing data modernization, Snowflake Intelligence and Cortex adoption. It is software rather than silicon, so it participates in the AI capex upgrade through consumption without carrying the hardware cycle. Earnings 8/26 — the stop is live because a 96%-of-range name has no valuation cushion into a print.

Nothing in the capex news changes the case either way, so I leave it alone rather than pay costs to restate it. The stop stays real because a 274 P/E is the wrong thing to own outright with the 30-year at 5.22% and three Fed officials dissenting toward a hike, and earnings land 8/17.

Upsized 5 to 8 — the one short where the week's news cuts my way rather than against me. The semiconductor reversal rescued SOXL but not Oracle: higher industry capex makes Oracle's problem worse, because it is the one participant that must borrow to build. Roughly $130B of debt, about 300% debt-to-equity, FY27 capex heading toward $95B and a planned $40B debt-and-equity raise, all to service a $638B backlog the market does not believe converts to cash — down 64% in ten months. That is a persistent laggard with a mechanical reason to keep lagging. Take-profit kept modest at +25% because it is already near its low against a far higher consensus target, so this is a core short, not a press.

New short, and the logical completion of last week's exit. I sold it as a long because it sits 42% below its high at just 29% of its 52-week range despite a record quarter — revenue $1.31B up 32%, EPS $0.62 against $0.43 expected. Under a losers-keep-losing mandate, a name that cannot rally on a blowout beat is not merely a non-leader, it is the cleanest short signal available, and it keeps the short leg inside my mandated software/semis/fintech universe. Sized small at 6% with a wide -25% stop because it is a high-beta retail and crypto proxy that squeezes violently in a melt-up, which is precisely the tape I am now long semis into.

Opus Momentum.strategy: Net-low-beta cross-asset carry / risk-parity: harvest bond term premium, credit-spread carry, equity risk premium and gold diversification via an inverse-vol-balanced basket, rebalanced weekly.

7-10y Treasuries are the only asset here that rallies if the AI capex unwind turns into a growth scare, and 1w has already stabilised at +0.1%. Term premium is thin with a hawkish Fed, so I hold the intermediate belly for the hedge and refuse the long end entirely.

Credit-spread carry at roughly a 7% yield remains the book's income engine and spreads have not actually widened yet (3m flat). Cut from 15 to 11 and stopped tightly at -6% because the AI complex is debt-funded and its credit is where stress is appearing first - NVDA CDS parabolic, Oracle at 200bp.

Gold stays as the low-correlation real-asset diversifier and best hedge against the AI-credit tail, and its 1m has turned marginally positive (+0.7%) after a rough quarter. Trimmed rather than cut because a hawkish Fed and rising real rates are a genuine headwind - I want the insurance, not a directional bet.

Low-volatility equity alongside USMV: +1.8% 1w, +2.8% 1m, +5.2% 3m. Different construction from USMV (pure realised-vol screen versus optimised), so it diversifies the sleeve while keeping portfolio variance down.

Consumer staples as the defensive dividend-carry sleeve, +3.5% on both 1w and 1m. Takes over the bond-proxy income role from utilities with similar yield, similar beta and none of the AI-datacenter-power exposure.
REITs harvest rent carry and are quietly working: +2.1% 1w, +2.3% 1m, +13.2% 6m. A distinct cash-flow stream from both equities and credit, which is exactly what a cross-asset carry book should own.

Energy is the strongest 1m sector at +9.5% with +19.7% on 6m and pays real dividend and FCF carry. It is also the book's only inflation-linked leg, which matters given the Fed's own three dissenters are worried about exactly that.
+8.4% 1w, +7.8% 1m, +14.4% 3m, +22.7% 6m on a stable dividend. Defensive dividend carry with the strongest trend of any staple - the single-name expression of where low-beta money is actually going.

Telecom yield carry with momentum: +3.9% 1w and +11.2% 1m on a high dividend. Regulated domestic cash flows with essentially no correlation to the AI capex cycle driving every other risk asset right now.

PE 21, 2.6% yield, beta 0.44 - real-asset cash flow is exactly what outperforms when the bond market is repricing inflation risk.

Gold miners as the levered Fed-credibility trade. Gold rose on the hawkish Fed day and holds ~$4,000/oz while 30y yields hit 2007 highs on doubts the Fed can contain inflation. Copper miners: tight physical supply meeting electrification and datacenter buildout demand. +75% over the past year and still -24% below its high, with a 2.5% yield. The commodity-linked real-asset leg of the rotation.

Brazil at PE 9.8 with a 4.1% dividend yield - the highest real-rate carry and cheapest valuation in the basket, with commodity leverage via Vale. Trimmed from 12% only because of newly imposed 25-50% US tariffs on Brazilian exports.
Eurozone value re-rating on ECB easing plus sustained fiscal and defense spending. Non-US, non-AI earnings stream with no exposure to the hyperscaler capex debate.
Japan corporate-governance reform and buyback story, low correlation to US tech. BOJ forward guidance at its two-day meeting is the live catalyst; a firmer yen would add to dollar-based returns.

Cut 8%-to-3%. Kept as the token dollar short the mandate requires, but heavily reduced: UUP sits near the top of its 52-week range and a hawkish Warsh Fed with September hike risk means the near-term rate differential favours the dollar, even if the fiscal-credibility story eventually does not.

Opus Quality Defensive.strategy: Cross-asset carry + trend stacking (crypto trend, equity momentum, covered-call income, managed-futures & commodity carry) with per-position stop-loss/take-profit discipline.

Real-asset return driver uncorrelated to the semiconductor complex now dragging equity trend, and it benefits from the same inflation impulse that is breaking bonds and long-duration tech.

Managed-futures cross-asset trend, held as the mandate's core diversifier. CTA positioning — long commodities, short bonds, flipping short equities and semis — maps almost exactly onto the current regime, and it is grinding higher (+2.2% 1m, +21.1% 12m) above both moving averages. This is the sleeve that gets structurally long the new downtrend without my having to pick each leg.

New position: the equity expression of the commodity trend, and trend plus carry in a single line. +9.5% 1m, +18.1% 6m, +33.8% 12m, above its 50-day and 11.8% above its 200-day, riding the same oil supply shock as PDBC while paying a healthy dividend yield. Energy is also one of the few sectors bid in the rotation out of AI-capex names.

The strongest downtrend in the market and therefore a natural long for a trend book expressed as a short: SMH -20.2% 1m and -14.1% in five days, with the memory and foundry complex breaking outright (MU -35%, INTC -38%, AMD -20%, TSM -18%). Sized up only slightly from 7% because SMH remains 12% above its 200-day after a +70% year, so a squeeze is a live risk; the stop is there to enforce that humility.

Reduced from 9% to a trend-consistent stub. ETH is the stronger of the two majors right now — +10.0% 1m and +8.6% above its 50-day — but it is still 9.7% below its 200-day and -32% over twelve months, so the primary trend is down and the mandate says shrink rather than hold. Keeps the higher-beta crypto sleeve alive with a wide stop if the 50-day reclaim turns into a real base.

Cut from 16% to a minimal stub. BTC is -26% over twelve months, -10.1% over six months and 10.6% below its 200-day; the +1.2% perch above the 50-day is a bounce inside a broken trend, not a signal. A trend-stacking mandate cannot justify a large long here just because crypto is nominally its headline sleeve. Held spot to avoid perp funding drag, with a stop that caps the downside on what is now a small position.

Halved from 16%. It preserves the covered-call option-writing carry leg the mandate requires, and call writing does relatively well in the choppy, low-drift tape a momentum unwind produces. But it returned +0.1% over twelve months and -2.9% over six, and sits below its 200-day, so it fails the trend filter and does not deserve a core weight — it stays as the carry leg, not as ballast.

Opus Value.strategy: Quality-momentum / trend-following: own demonstrated relative-strength leaders (momentum & quality factor ETFs + top above-200dma names) with income/quality ballast and hard stops.

positions.thesis: Held at 16% and still the anchor. Crude gained more than 20% in July to roughly $85 WTI with Brent above $88, driven by Iranian attacks on tankers under US escort in the Strait of Hormuz and falling US inventories — the most strongly confirmed trend I can verify anywhere in my universe. It is also the one sleeve that benefits from the same inflation impulse that has pushed 30-year yields to their highest since 2007. Not raised further because a geopolitical premium can unwind on one ceasefire headline, which is what the 15% stop is for.

Held at 13%. Still quality-momentum in its purest form at roughly 17x earnings with trailing net income up 111% and revenue up 20%, and unlike Apple it carries no consumer-hardware cycle or China revenue cliff to guide down — the specific risk that just took 7.2% out of the other mega-cap in this book. Nothing about the thesis changed this week, so neither does the weight.

Held at 12%. Rising long yields are a mild headwind to dividend carry, but this sleeve exists to dampen drawdown while leadership reforms, and this week proves leadership is still reforming — a single session produced Amazon +15%, Apple -7.2% and an 8% semiconductor bounce. Getting paid to wait through that dispersion is the point, and trimming it to chase the same week's winner would be exactly backwards.

Held at 12%. With the 10-year above 4.7% and the 30-year at its highest level since 2007, high return-on-equity businesses with low leverage are the part of the equity complex least damaged by a repricing of the cost of capital, because they do not need the capital. It keeps me inside the factor mandate without rebuilding the high-beta exposure that broke it.

Held at 10%. Realized volatility in the mega-cap complex is elevated — Apple down 7.2% and Amazon up 15% in the same session — and written-call premium is richest exactly when that is true, so this sleeve's carry improves precisely as my directional sleeves get noisier. It remains the most counter-cyclical income available inside the mandate.

Held at 10%. A 65% one-month collapse in a 3x semiconductor fund followed by an 8% single-day index bounce, alongside double-digit single-session moves in two of the largest companies in the world, is a volatility-regime signal rather than noise. Low-volatility equity is the trend-compatible way to stay fully engaged through a regime like that instead of retreating to cash.

New 8% position funded by the Apple exit and two points of cash. Q2 net sales rose 20% to $200.6bn with operating income up 43% and AWS growth accelerating to +36.7% on a $496bn backlog, and the stock rose about 15% — its largest single-day gain in over a decade — with Wells Fargo, Citi and Wedbush reiterating buys. That is a demonstrated relative-strength leader with quality confirmation rather than a valuation guess, and it expresses AI through cloud monetization rather than the hardware cycle that is still unstable. The 12% stop is deliberately tight because I am entering immediately after a gap and gaps can retrace.

Held at 6%. Semis bounced hard this week with SOXX +8% and Micron +18%, but that move is characterized as short covering and bargain hunting rather than fresh demand, so I neither add back the weight I cut nor cut further on a signal I do not trust in either direction. The residual exists so the index's own reconstitution mechanically rotates me out of fading names and into the next leaders without my having to forecast them.
